NO. 012 · Coast & Tidal Flats / Scolopacidae · Sandpipers & Snipes

Dunlin

黑腹滨鹬 · hēi fù bīn yù Calidris alpina
Winter visitor Abundant 17–21 cm Protected (China) IUCN LC

The most numerous small sandpiper on the flats

On a Pearl River Delta flat in winter, hundreds of small waders move like a grey cloud — and most of them are Dunlins. They sprint low, turn as one, and look choreographed.

Gallery

One scientific illustration for shape and colour blocks, two field photographs for how it looks in real light. Click any image to enlarge.

Identification

  • BillBlack, fairly long and clearly downcurved, the tip soft and flexible with dense touch receptors — built for probing mud.
  • PlumageIn non-breeding plumage grey-brown above and white below with fine streaking on the breast sides and flanks; in breeding plumage a large black belly patch appears — the 'dun' of the name.
  • LegsBlack and short, made for running on mud.
  • FlockExtremely gregarious, often hundreds packed together, turning in unison in flight so the flock flashes light and dark.

Behaviour

A typical flocking wader of the flats, moving with the tide: it gathers on high ground as the water rises and spreads across the mud as it falls. Probes repeatedly in the sediment for small snails, worms and crustaceans. A winter visitor here and one of the most numerous waders in the region.

Where to find it in Zhuhai

  • Jinwan tidal flats
  • Qi'ao Island tidal flats
  • Hengqin coastal mudflats
  • Doumen coast
Field note
Judge by the flock: tens of birds may be another sandpiper; a grey cloud of hundreds is almost certainly Dunlin. At close range look for the clearly downcurved bill and the fine streaking on the breast sides.
